introduction.p: A Taylor series may fail to represent its defining function, and convergence inside an interval does not decide endpoint behavior. Also, term-by-term differentiation and integration require hypotheses on convergence. The examples below distinguish these failures.

note.title: Moral
note.p: The Taylor series is built from derivative data at one point. That data can be insufficient. To prove that a Taylor series equals a function, we need the remainder to satisfy

subsection.p: This is why Taylor’s theorem was not optional bookkeeping. The remainder is the bridge between the Taylor polynomials and the function.

exercise.title: Why can a Taylor series converge without equaling the function?

statement.p: The flat function that is e^{-1/x^2} away from 0 has every derivative zero at the origin, so its Taylor series is identically zero. In your own words, why does that show that derivative data at one point can be insufficient, and what extra statement is needed before the series is the function?

hint.p: The Taylor series records only the derivatives at the center. If those derivatives cannot see the function, the series cannot either. The remainder must tend to zero.

subsection.title: Endpoint behavior differs from interior behavior
subsection.p: Inside the radius of convergence, power series behave predictably. They converge absolutely. They can be differentiated and integrated term by term.

paragraphs.title: Integration can gain endpoints
paragraphs.p: The original geometric series diverges at both endpoints. The integrated series converges at x=-1 by the Alternating Series Test, but diverges at x=1 as the harmonic series.

note.title: Endpoint rule
note.p: Differentiation and integration preserve the radius of convergence, but they do not preserve endpoint behavior.
After any term-by-term operation, test endpoints again.

exercise.title: Why is endpoint behavior not decided by the interior?

statement.p: Differentiation and integration preserve radius but not endpoint behavior. In your own words, why can the interior be completely safe while an endpoint still requires a fresh numerical test, and why should every term-by-term operation be followed by that test?

hint.p: Inside the radius there is a geometric margin. An endpoint sits exactly where that margin vanishes, so a new series may gain or lose an endpoint even though R is unchanged.

paragraphs.title: Differentiation has its own warning
paragraphs.p: Even uniform convergence of functions is not enough to justify differentiating limits.

So differentiating the approximating functions did not guarantee differentiability of the limit. To pass derivatives through a limit or an infinite sum, we need extra control, usually control of the derivative series itself.

note.title: Moral
note.p: Pointwise convergence is usually too weak for term-by-term operations.
Power series are special because they converge uniformly on every closed interval strictly inside their radius of convergence.

exercise.title: Why do term-by-term operations need hypotheses?

statement.p: Arbitrary series of functions can fail to pass integrals or derivatives through the limit, even when each approximant is well behaved. In your own words, why is pointwise convergence usually too weak, and why are power series special inside their radius?

hint.p: Passing an integral or a derivative through a limit is an interval-wide claim. Power series earn that claim by uniform geometric control on compact subintervals of the open interval of convergence.

subsection.title: A good local approximation can become bad far away
subsection.p: Taylor polynomials are local approximations. They are built from derivative information at one center. A polynomial that is excellent near the center can be useless far away.

warning.title: Local approximation warning
warning.p: A Taylor polynomial may be excellent near its center and poor far away.
A Taylor series may represent a function only on part of the function’s domain.

subsection.p: A power-series calculation needs a specified domain, convergence justification, and an applicable remainder estimate. Without these, formal manipulations may not establish an identity or an accurate approximation.

exercise.title: Why can a good local approximation become useless far away?

statement.p: The geometric partial sums approach 1/(1-x) for |x|<1, but at x=2 they explode while the function is perfectly defined. In your own words, why is a Taylor polynomial a local object, and why does existence of the function at a far point not license using the series there?

hint.p: A Taylor polynomial is built from data at one center, but being a polynomial it is defined everywhere. Its accuracy away from that center needs a remainder estimate. The associated infinite Taylor series has its own convergence radius and need not represent the function beyond it.
